title: How the bishop moves
summary: Diagonals any distance; a bishop stays on its starting colour for the whole game.

steps.md: The **bishop** moves diagonally, any number of empty squares, and cannot jump. Because it only moves diagonally it **never changes square colour**: each side has one light-squared and one dark-squared bishop. Value: about 3 pawns.
From d4 the bishop sweeps both diagonals: a1-h8 and a7-g1. 13 squares, all dark.

steps.explain: One move along the long a1-h8 diagonal.
Backwards along the a7-g1 diagonal. Beginners often miss backward bishop moves, so look for them on purpose.

steps.question: The bishop is on d4, a dark square. Can it ever reach e4?
choices: No, e4 is a light square
steps.explain: e4 is light. A dark-squared bishop can never reach a light square, however many moves it makes.

steps.prompt: Bring the bishop from c1 to c5 in two moves. Your own pawn on d2 blocks one diagonal.
steps.hint: Go out to the a-file first.
steps.explain: With d2 blocked, the only route is c1-a3-c5. Bishops often need a zig-zag to reach a square on the same file.

steps.question: How many squares does a bishop on d4 control on an empty board, compared with one in the corner (a1)?
steps.explain: Centralised bishops are stronger: 13 squares on d4, only 7 from the corner. Rooks always have 14, but bishops gain from the centre.

steps.question: Retrieval check: why can a bishop never change square colour?
choices: Every diagonal step lands on the same colour
It is a special rule for bishops
steps.explain: Moving one step diagonally keeps you on the same colour, so the bishop is locked to its starting colour.

steps.question: Retrieval check: each side starts with...
choices: one light-squared and one dark-squared bishop
steps.explain: c1 is dark and f1 is light for White (f8 dark and c8 light for Black).
